summary: This Best Current Practice defines a syntax called a language-range for listing a user's language preferences, and two ways to match those against language tags: filtering, which returns a set, and lookup, which returns one tag. With RFC 4646 it replaced RFC 3066.

eli5.summary: If you say you like English and then French, a site needs a way to pick what you get. This explains how to match your list against what the site has.

questions: what is the difference between filtering and lookup
subtitle: How to write down a user's language preferences and match them against language tags, by filtering for a set or by lookup for one best answer.

tldr.problem: Applications that label content with language tags also need to compare those tags to what a user prefers, and different needs call for different kinds of matching.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4647 defines the language range, a pattern of subtags with an optional wildcard, and a prioritized list of such ranges. It then defines three matching schemes: basic filtering, extended filtering and lookup.
tldr.outcome: Filtering returns a possibly empty set of tags and lookup returns exactly one. Any protocol that uses this RFC must say which scheme it uses and what happens when nothing matches. With RFC 5646 it replaced RFC 3066.

today: RFC 4647 is a Best Current Practice published in September 2006. The unit metadata records that it obsoletes RFC 3066 and lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It forms BCP 47 together with RFC 5646, the revision of the language tag specification.

sections.title: Why Tags Need Matching
sections.content:
Applications often need to compare the language tags on content, as defined in RFC 4646, with a user's language preferences. This document defines a syntax for one item in those preferences, called a language range, and for the whole list, called a language priority list. It also defines several schemes for selecting or filtering language tags by comparing them to the user's preferences.

The RFC is a Best Current Practice. Together with RFC 4646 it replaces RFC 3066, which had replaced RFC 1766. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as described in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: Tags are labels on things, such as 'this is in German'. This RFC is about checking a person's wish list against those labels.

sections.title: Language Ranges and Priority Lists
sections.content:
A language range looks like a language tag: subtags separated by hyphens. In a range each subtag MUST be either a run of ASCII letters and digits or the single character *, a wildcard that matches any sequence of subtags. Ranges and tags are case-insensitive, and matching MUST be done that way.

A basic language range has the same syntax as an RFC 3066 tag, or is just *. Unlike a tag from RFC 4646 it does not have to be well-formed or validated against the IANA Language Subtag Registry, so an ill-formed range will probably match nothing. An extended language range is an ordered sequence of subtags in which a wildcard may appear in any position. It lets a user ask, for example, for every tag that contains the region subtag CH without naming the subtags in between.

A language priority list is a prioritized or weighted list of ranges. A speaker of Breton in France could give br followed by fr, meaning Breton if available and French otherwise. This document does not define the syntax of such a list; the protocol that uses it does, as the Accept-Language header with its q values does in HTTP. Examples here are written as a quoted, comma-separated list such as en, fr, zh-Hant, read as English before French before Traditional-script Chinese.
sections.eli5: A language range is a short pattern, like 'anything that starts with German'. A priority list is your wish list: first choice, second choice, and so on.

sections.title: Three Matching Schemes
sections.content:
A scheme that can produce zero or more matching tags is called filtering. A scheme that produces exactly one match for a request is called lookup. The RFC describes three schemes. Basic filtering matches basic ranges to sets of tags, extended filtering does the same with extended ranges, and lookup matches basic ranges to find the one tag that best fits. A protocol that claims conformance MUST clearly say which mechanism it uses.

Filtering suits cases such as limiting search results to items tagged as French, or deciding whether to italicize paragraphs matching the range nl (Dutch). Lookup suits cases where only one item can be returned, such as choosing the text of an error message to put into a protocol header. Because it must return something, it has to choose an item even when no tag matches the user's list.
sections.eli5: Filtering is like asking for every book in French. Lookup is like asking for one book to read right now, so you have to leave with something.

sections.title: How Filtering Works
sections.content:
In filtering, each range stands for the least specific tag that is an acceptable match. Every matching tag has at least as many subtags as the range, and every non-wildcard subtag of the range appears in it. The range de-CH can match de-CH-1996 but never plain de. Results are typically ordered by descending preference but MAY be unordered. The RFC cautions that tags sharing a prefix are not necessarily mutually intelligible.

Basic filtering considers each range in turn, by priority. A range matches a tag if, compared case-insensitively, it equals the tag or equals a prefix of the tag whose next character is a hyphen. So de-de matches de-DE-1996 but not de-Deva or de-Latn-DE. The special range * matches any tag, although a protocol MAY add rules for it.

Extended filtering splits both the range and the tag into subtags and walks along them. The first subtags must match, where a wildcard in the range matches anything. For each remaining range subtag, the process skips a wildcard, fails if the tag has run out, advances both if they match, fails if the tag's subtag is a singleton (a single letter or digit, including x), and otherwise skips ahead in the tag. When the range runs out, the match succeeds. The range de-*-DE (equivalent to de-DE) matches de-Latn-DE, de-DE-x-goethe and de-Deva-DE. It does not match de, de-x-DE or de-Deva. Because subtag types depend on position, a wildcard matters in the first position and is ignored elsewhere.
sections.eli5: Filtering keeps everything that starts the way you asked. Asking for 'German in Germany' also keeps 'German in Germany in the 1996 spelling', but not plain 'German', because it never says Germany.

sections.title: How Lookup and Defaults Work
sections.content:
Lookup returns the single tag that best matches the priority list. Here each range stands for the most specific tag that is acceptable, so the range de-ch can yield content tagged de or de-CH but never de-CH-1996. The first match found, in the user's priority order, is returned. Lookup works by progressively truncating the range from the end until a match is found. Single-letter or digit subtags, including x, are removed together with their closest trailing subtag.

The range * is skipped if other ranges follow it, and if it is the only range or comes last, the default value is computed and returned. When extended ranges reach lookup, the protocol MUST define which item is returned if more than one matches. Mapping them to basic ranges is one option, and returning the first tag in ASCII order is another.

Every protocol that uses lookup MUST define what happens when nothing matches. Examples include returning an item with no language tag, an empty value where the protocol permits it, a designated tag, the tag i-default, an error, or a list of available languages. The search MUST work through every range in the list before the default is sought. If a default range is configured, it MUST be treated as if appended to the end of the whole list, not after each item.
sections.eli5: Lookup starts with your most exact wish and keeps dropping details until something fits. If nothing fits, it hands you the standard choice.

sections.title: Rules for Protocol Designers
sections.content:
Matching is a tool, not a complete procedure. A protocol that uses it MUST specify which types of matching it uses, whether the operation returns a single result or a possibly empty set, and for lookup what the default is when nothing matches. Implementations are not required to validate or understand the tags, or to have the IANA Language Subtag Registry, which keeps them simple. Designers are encouraged to use the registry to canonicalize tags and ranges, mapping grandfathered and obsolete forms to modern ones. An implementation that canonicalizes ranges MUST either match using both the canonical and original form of the range or also canonicalize each tag. Canonicalizing has a cost: a range art-lojban rewritten to jbo can no longer select only items with the older tag.

An application that uses basic ranges may receive extended ones. It MUST choose to map them to basic ranges, reject those that are not valid basic ranges, or treat them as basic ranges, which amounts to ignoring them. The mapping treats a range with a wildcard first as * and otherwise deletes each wildcard, so en-*-US becomes en-US.
sections.eli5: Anyone building a system with these rules has to write down which kind of matching they use and what to do when nothing fits, so everyone gets the same answer.

sections.title: Choosing Good Ranges
sections.content:
Most schemes compare tags as plain strings, case-insensitively, without looking at what the subtags mean. Users SHOULD pick ranges that are well-formed, valid tags from RFC 4646. They should avoid subtags that add no distinguishing value. When filtering, fewer subtags match more content, while in lookup extra subtags can cause better content to be skipped. For example, the range de-Latn-DE returns content tagged de instead of de-DE.

A user who reads Simplified and Traditional Chinese but prefers Simplified might use zh for filtering and zh-Hans for lookup. If unsure which scheme will be used, the user SHOULD list the most specific range first and shorter prefixes later, as in zh-Hans, zh. Script subtags SHOULD NOT be used when the language's registry entry has a Suppress-Script field for that script, so en-Latn is usually inappropriate. Extensions and private-use subtags should be avoided in ranges, and the RFC advises great caution with private-use subtags in general, since they are useless for exchange without prior arrangement.
sections.eli5: Ask for exactly as much detail as you need. Too many details can make you miss a good match, and too few can bring back things you cannot read.

sections.title: Privacy and Character Sets
sections.content:
Language ranges used in content negotiation might be used to infer the nationality of the sender, and so identify potential targets for surveillance. Unique or highly unusual ranges, or combinations of them, might be used to track a specific individual. The RFC calls this a special case of the general problem that anything you send is visible to the receiving party, and leaves the size of the threat and any countermeasures to each application or protocol.

On character sets, tags use only A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and the hyphen-minus, and ranges also use the asterisk. These characters exist in most character sets, so character set issues should not constrain their exchange.
sections.eli5: Telling a website which languages you like also tells it a little about you, so it is worth knowing that.
